seo_title: Why Flashing Is Commonly Missed in Roof Insurance Claims
meta_description: Learn why flashing is commonly missed in claims, which step, chimney, and valley items get left out, and how to fix your roof estimate. Free claim review.
h1: Why Flashing Is Commonly Missed in Roof Insurance Claims
excerpt: Step, counter, valley, and chimney flashing are among the most overlooked items in roof claims. Learn why they get missed and how to get them added to your estimate.
key_takeaways: Flashing is hidden under shingles, so inspections and aerial reports often miss it.
Estimates frequently assume flashing can be reused, even when tear-off will damage it.
Manufacturer instructions and local codes can require new flashing and drip edge.
Flashing scope disputes are amount-of-loss issues that appraisal can resolve.
body_html:
Flashing is commonly missed in roof insurance claims because it is hidden under shingles, damage to it is hard to see from the ground or in aerial photos, and adjusters often assume old metal can be reused. Missing step, counter, valley, chimney, and pipe flashing leaves homeowners with supplements, leaks, and out-of-pocket costs.

Shingles get the attention on a hail or wind claim. They are visible, they show bruising and creasing, and they make up most of the roof's surface. Flashing is the quiet partner: the metal and boots that seal every place the roof changes direction or meets a wall, chimney, or penetration.

When an estimate leaves flashing out, the problem usually surfaces during tear-off, when the roofer discovers that the existing metal cannot be reused or was never installed correctly. This guide explains why flashing gets missed, which items to look for, and how to fix the gap before repairs begin.

What Is Roof Flashing and Why Does It Matter?

Roof flashing is thin metal (or, at pipes, rubber or lead boots) installed at joints and transitions to direct water away from vulnerable seams. Shingles shed water across open slopes, but they cannot seal an intersection by themselves. Flashing fills that role.

Common types of roof flashing

Flashing typeWhere it goesWhat it does
Step flashingWhere a sloped roof meets a sidewallIndividual L-shaped pieces woven into each shingle course
Counter (cap) flashingOver step flashing at walls and chimneysCovers the top edge of step flashing and seals into masonry or siding
Chimney flashingAround all four sides of a chimneyIncludes apron, step, counter, and often a cricket on the high side
Valley flashingWhere two roof planes meet in a valleyChannels heavy water flow in open metal valleys
Pipe boots / jacksAround plumbing ventsSeal the penetration; rubber collars crack with age and heat
Drip edgeAlong eaves and rakesDirects water off the roof edge and protects fascia and decking
Skylight flashing kitsAround skylightsManufacturer-specific systems that integrate with shingles

Even though these components represent a small share of a roof's cost, they protect the areas most likely to leak.

Why Is Flashing Commonly Missed in Insurance Claims?

Flashing omissions are rarely the result of a single mistake. Several factors tend to stack up.

Inspections focus on visible shingle damage

An adjuster working through a test square looks for hail hits and wind creases on shingles. Flashing is tucked under courses or behind siding, so storm damage to it may not be visible without lifting shingles or getting close at the wall line.

Aerial and drone imagery cannot see under shingles

Measurement reports are excellent for area, pitch, and linear footage, but they cannot show whether step flashing is bent, corroded, or missing. If the estimate is built mostly from an aerial report, flashing details often fall through the cracks.

The "reuse" assumption

Many estimates assume existing flashing can be carefully removed and reinstalled. In practice, step flashing is woven into each course and often gets bent or torn during tear-off. Counter flashing may be embedded in mortar joints or sealed behind siding. Pipe boots are frequently brittle after years of Texas sun.

High claim volume after storms

After a major hail event in North or Central Texas, adjusters can handle a very large number of claims in a short window. Speed favors the obvious items. Detailed flashing scopes take time, and time is scarce during catastrophe response. Our article on why insurance companies underscope roof damage explains this pattern more broadly.

Tip: Ask your adjuster directly whether the estimate assumes flashing will be reused. A written answer gives you a clear starting point for a supplement if the roofer finds otherwise.

Which Flashing Items Are Most Often Left Out?

From the policyholder side, these are the flashing line items we most often find missing or underscoped on Texas roof claims:

  • Step flashing at sidewalls, especially on two-story homes where roof planes meet siding or brick.
  • Counter flashing and reglet work at chimneys and masonry walls, including cutting and resealing into mortar.
  • Chimney crickets on wider chimneys, which may need to be rebuilt along with their flashing.
  • Valley metal on roofs designed with open metal valleys.
  • Pipe jacks and vent flashing, including lead boots and the labor to remove and replace them.
  • Drip edge at eaves and rakes, which local building codes often require on a new roof.
  • Skylight flashing kits required by the skylight manufacturer.
  • Siding or stucco detach and reset needed to access step and counter flashing properly.

Many of these appear in our list of common Xactimate line items missing from roof claims.

What Does Storm-Damaged Flashing Look Like?

Knowing what to look for helps you separate storm damage from ordinary aging, which is often the first argument an adjuster raises.

  • Hail dents and splits on exposed metal such as counter flashing, valley metal, chimney caps, and vent hoods. Soft metals often show round dents that line up with hail hits elsewhere on the property.
  • Bent or lifted edges where high winds caught exposed flashing or peeled back shingles and the metal beneath them.
  • Torn or punctured pipe boots, which hail can split, especially when the rubber is already stiff from heat.
  • Displaced counter flashing pulled out of mortar joints or away from siding.
  • Interior water stains near walls, chimneys, or skylights that appear soon after a storm.

Dented metal is also useful evidence for the whole claim. Adjusters and appraisers commonly look at collateral damage to soft metals, such as flashing, gutters, and vents, to help confirm hail size and direction. Photograph these dents with a chalk circle or a coin for scale before anything is repaired.

Not every flashing problem is storm-related. Rust, failed sealant, and improper original installation may be treated as maintenance or construction defects. That is why good documentation matters: it lets an appraiser or umpire separate what the storm did from what was already there.

How Manufacturer Instructions and Building Codes Affect Flashing

Two factors can turn a "reuse" assumption into a required replacement.

Manufacturer installation instructions

Shingle manufacturers publish detailed installation instructions, including how flashing must be installed at walls, valleys, and penetrations. Contractors who install a new roof are expected to follow them, and warranty coverage may depend on it. If the existing flashing does not meet those instructions, reusing it may not be an option.

Local building codes

Most Texas cities adopt a version of the International Residential Code, which addresses flashing at walls, valleys, chimneys, and roof edges and, in recent editions, drip edge at eaves and rakes. When a full re-roof triggers current code, items the old roof never had may be required. Whether your policy pays for those upgrades depends on your coverage; see ordinance and law coverage explained.

How Missing Flashing Affects Homeowners

A flashing omission costs more than the price of the metal.

  • Leak risk. If the roofer reuses damaged flashing to stay within the insurance scope, the new roof may leak at the very spots flashing was supposed to protect.
  • Out-of-pocket costs. Contractors who discover the problem mid-job need to be paid for the extra work, and the supplement may take weeks.
  • Project delays. Waiting on a re-inspection or supplement approval can leave a roof partially open or a job stalled.
  • Interior damage later. Slow leaks at walls and chimneys can rot decking and framing before they show up on a ceiling.

Flashing Problems on Texas Hail and Wind Claims

Texas weather is hard on flashing. Large hail can dent and split exposed metal, high straight-line winds lift shingle edges and the flashing beneath, and intense summer heat dries out rubber pipe boots. Older homes in Fort Worth, Waco, and San Antonio frequently have masonry chimneys and brick sidewalls that require careful counter flashing work during a re-roof.

Along the Gulf Coast, wind-driven rain during tropical storms tests every transition on a roof. The National Weather Service storm reports for your area and date of loss can help document that a damaging event occurred.

How to Document Missing or Damaged Flashing

  1. Photograph every transition: walls, chimneys, valleys, skylights, and pipes, with close-ups and wide shots.
  2. Measure linear footage of sidewalls, chimney perimeters, valleys, and eaves.
  3. Get a contractor's written scope explaining why the flashing cannot be reused.
  4. Save tear-off photos if hidden problems are discovered during installation, before the area is covered.
  5. Cite manufacturer instructions or local code when they require replacement.

Our free claim documentation checklist lists everything worth collecting. Matterport 3D scans and drone imagery can also capture roof transitions in detail before work starts.

Can Appraisal Resolve a Flashing Dispute?

Usually, yes. When the insurer agrees the roof has covered storm damage but disputes whether flashing should be replaced, that is a disagreement about the scope and amount of loss. That is exactly what the appraisal clause in most Texas policies is designed to settle.

In appraisal, your appraiser prepares a line-item estimate that includes the flashing work needed to restore the roof properly and supports it with photos, measurements, and manufacturer or code references. If the two appraisers cannot agree, an umpire decides. Learn more in our guide to using appraisal for roof claims.

Next Steps Before You Accept a Roof Estimate

  • Search the estimate for step flashing, counter flashing, valley metal, pipe jacks, and drip edge.
  • Compare linear footage to your roof's sidewalls, chimney, and edges.
  • Ask whether the scope assumes flashing reuse, and get the answer in writing.
  • Have your roofer flag any flashing that cannot be reused before work starts.
  • Submit a documented supplement, and consider appraisal if the insurer will not move.

faqs.q: Is roof flashing covered by homeowners insurance?
faqs.a: Flashing damaged by a covered peril such as hail or wind is generally covered like the rest of the roof. Flashing that must be replaced to complete a covered roof replacement is also commonly included. Wear, corrosion from age, or poor original installation may be excluded. Check your policy and ask the adjuster how flashing was handled in the estimate.

faqs.q: Can step flashing be reused when a roof is replaced?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but often not. Step flashing is woven into each shingle course, so removing it without bending or tearing it is difficult. Many roofers replace it during a re-roof, and manufacturer instructions may affect the decision. If the insurer's estimate assumes reuse and the roofer finds damaged flashing during tear-off, document it with photos and submit a supplement.

faqs.q: Why wasn't drip edge included in my roof estimate?
faqs.a: Drip edge is a separate line item measured in linear feet, so it is easy to leave out. Some estimates omit it because the old roof had none. Many Texas cities have adopted building codes that call for drip edge on new roofs. Whether the upgrade is paid depends on your policy's code or ordinance and law coverage.

faqs.q: How do I add missing flashing to my insurance claim?
faqs.a: Gather photos of every wall, chimney, valley, and pipe transition, plus linear measurements and a contractor's written explanation of why new flashing is needed. Submit this to the adjuster as a supplement request and ask for a written response. If the insurer agrees the roof is covered but still refuses the flashing work, appraisal can resolve the disagreement.
